title: Never Disparaging (Kern ch. 19)
hook: a bodhisattva bows to everyone: I don't despise you, you will become a Buddha; they throw stones, he bows from further off

segments.voice: Yesterday, the preacher's senses: the same eyes and ears, made clear. Your line: clear senses. Did you hear someone's whole voice before you answered? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-five.

A monk walks up to a stranger on the road, bows low, and says: I don't despise you. You will become a Buddha. The stranger stares at him. Then gets angry. Who asked this man for his opinion? A stick comes up, or a handful of stones. The monk steps back, out of range, and says it again, louder, from further off. That is very nearly the whole story of chapter nineteen in Kern's numbering, and the chapter says it went on like that for a long time. Today: Never Disparaging.
screen: `A BOW ON THE ROAD.` → `A HANDFUL OF STONES.` → `SAID AGAIN, FROM FURTHER OFF.`

segments.voice: First, the monk. The Buddha tells of a time long ago, after an ancient Buddha had passed away, when arrogant monks held sway. There was a bodhisattva monk who did not spend his days reciting scriptures. Whenever he saw anyone, monk or nun, layman or laywoman, he went up, bowed, and said the same thing: I do not despise you. You are walking the bodhisattva path, and you will become Buddhas. Second, why it angered people. Some heard it as an insult wrapped in a compliment. Who was he to make predictions about them? They shouted at him and struck at him with sticks and clods of earth. Third, what he did. He stepped away, out of reach, and called the same words back from a distance. He did not change his line, and he did not strike back. That is how he got his name. In the Chinese translation, the name is Never Disparaging. Some readers hear two things at once in the Sanskrit name, Sadaparibhuta: the one who never despised, and the one who was always despised. Fourth, who he turned out to be. Near the end of his life, the chapter says, he heard the Lotus Sutra, his senses were made clear, the very thing yesterday described, and his life was lengthened so he could teach it. Those who had mocked him came to listen. Then the Buddha tells the assembly: that monk was me. And some of the people who once threw the stones are sitting here now.
screen: `A MONK WHO ONLY BOWS.` · `HEARD AS AN INSULT.` · `HE STEPS BACK AND SAYS IT AGAIN.` · `THAT MONK WAS ME.` · then, large: `I DO NOT DESPISE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: bow inwardly to everyone you meet. Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind, one at a time, people you are likely to see today: someone at home, someone at work, a stranger behind a counter. For each, let there be a small inward bow. No movement, just a slight dip of attention, as if to say: I see you. Then bring to mind one person who is hard for you. Notice whatever comes. Offer the same small bow, from as far off as you need. The bell holds the time.
Never Disparaging. In the Lotus Sutra, the monk who bowed to everyone and told them they would become Buddhas, and who, the Buddha says, was himself in a past life. Today's word.
Your line: I do not despise you. Today, when someone irritates you, let the line run once in your head before you answer. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: In Tendai and Nichiren Buddhism, Never Disparaging is held up as a model for practice in hard times, and some practitioners bow to others as a reminder that everyone can become a Buddha.

fork.setup: you have bowed to a stranger and said, 'I do not despise you; you will become a Buddha.' they pick up a stick. what do you do?
options: stop saying it; it only causes trouble
step back out of reach and say it again
fork.reveal: the monk neither struck back nor gave up: he moved out of range and called the same words from further off, for a long time.

original.note: Sanskrit: the monk's name; the Chinese translation calls him Never Disparaging.

trapdoor: what you thought: Never Disparaging is just a polite name.
what it means: a monk who bowed to everyone and told them they would become Buddhas, and kept saying it while they struck at him.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear both 'never despising' and 'always despised' in the Sanskrit name Sadaparibhuta; the chapter itself ties the name to his one message.

notes: Paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884), ch. 19; nothing quoted. The monk's words are given in paraphrase without quotation marks.
Check the name readings: Sadaparibhuta as 'always despised' / 'never despising', and 'Never Disparaging' as the Chinese (Kumarajiva) rendering. Kept as 'can be read' and 'some readers'.

Check: setting after a past Buddha's extinction when arrogant monks prevailed; sticks and clods; hearing the sutra near death, purified senses, lengthened life; the Buddha's identification with the monk; persecutors in the present assembly.
howItsDone: Tendai and Nichiren use of the figure kept general; Keeper to confirm.
